16.text:
## Background
Leviticus is traditionally attributed to Moses, and its setting is Mount Sinai after the tabernacle has been built. Most of the book was written for Israel's priests, explaining how a holy God could live among an imperfect people. Chapter 16 sits near the middle of the book and describes its most solemn ritual: the Day of Atonement, still kept by Jewish people today as Yom Kippur. The chapter opens by recalling the deaths of Aaron's two sons, who came before the Lord in the wrong way. That tragedy is the reason for the careful instructions that follow.

## What happens
God warns Aaron not to enter the inner room behind the veil, where the ark and its mercy seat stand, whenever he likes, or he will die, because God appears there in the cloud (vv. 1–2). Aaron must prepare with a bull for his own sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering. He must bathe and wear plain linen garments rather than his splendid robes (vv. 3–4). From the people he takes two goats and a ram (v. 5).

Lots are cast over the two goats. One is "for the LORD" and will be sacrificed, and the other is "for the scapegoat" and is kept alive (vv. 7–10). Aaron first deals with his own sin. He kills the bull, carries burning coals and incense behind the veil so that smoke covers the mercy seat, and sprinkles the bull's blood on and before it seven times (vv. 11–14). Then he does the same with the blood of the people's goat (v. 15). This cleanses the sanctuary itself from Israel's uncleanness and sins, and then the altar outside (vv. 16–19). No one else may be in the tent while he does this (v. 17).

Next comes the live goat. Aaron lays both hands on its head, confesses all Israel's sins over it, and a designated man leads it away into the wilderness, "unto a land not inhabited" (vv. 20–22). Aaron then removes the linen garments, washes, and offers the burnt offerings (vv. 23–25). The men who release the goat and burn the remains outside the camp must wash before returning (vv. 26–28).

Finally the day is made permanent. Every year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, everyone, including foreigners living among Israel, must rest and "afflict your souls," because on that day they are cleansed "from all your sins before the LORD" (vv. 29–34).

## Key words and ideas
- Mercy seat: the gold lid of the ark of the covenant. The Hebrew word is related to the verb for making atonement, so this is the place where sin is dealt with in God's presence.
- Atonement: in this chapter it means cleansing and covering. Notice that it applies not only to people but also to the holy place, the tabernacle and the altar, which have been polluted by living "in the midst of their uncleanness" (v. 16).
- Scapegoat: the Hebrew word here is azazel. Its meaning is debated. It may mean "the goat that goes away," the name of a remote place, or a wilderness being. Whatever the exact sense, the picture is clear: sin is carried far away.
- Afflict your souls: this has traditionally been understood as fasting and humbling oneself before God.

## Connections
The warning in verses 1–2 looks back to Leviticus 10:1–2, where Nadab and Abihu die after offering "strange fire." Hebrews 9:7–8 and Hebrews 9:25 describe this yearly entry of the high priest, and Hebrews 10:19–20 says believers may now enter the holy place through Jesus' blood, "through the veil." Hebrews 9:22–23 echoes the cleansing of the sanctuary with blood. The laying of sins on the goat finds an echo in Isaiah 53:6, "the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all," and in 2 Corinthians 5:21. Psalm 51:2 and Jeremiah 33:8 share the chapter's longing to be washed clean. Christians of all traditions read this chapter through Hebrews. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often connect Christ's one sacrifice with the Eucharist, while many Protestants stress that it was finished once for all. Jewish readers keep Yom Kippur with repentance, prayer and fasting.

## For reflection
- What does it suggest that even the high priest needed atonement before he could help anyone else?
- How does the image of sin being carried "unto a land not inhabited" speak to you?
- Why might God want a whole community, strangers included, to stop work and humble themselves together?
